title: Optimal Learning-Augmented Algorithm for Online Bidding
claim: Our method achieves a provably optimal robustness-consistency trade-off, closing the gap between prior upper and lower bounds in two settings.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-scale line plots, shared axes, legend boxes inside each panel
description: Two side-by-side line plots with gridlines, both plotting robustness (y-axis) against consistency (x-axis). Panel (a), online bidding, has a boxed legend and five items. The solid blue curve is the paper's algorithm, which also serves as the lower bound. The dashed orange curve is a prior lower bound that sits just below it. The dash-dotted red and dotted brown curves are prior algorithms that lie well above the blue curve. A purple dot at (e, e) marks the classical algorithm without predictions. Panel (b), linear search, has the same layout. The solid blue curve is the new algorithm and the dashed teal curve is the new lower bound just beneath it. The dotted brown curve is a prior algorithm far above both. A purple dot at ρ*_LS marks the classical algorithm. The eye goes first to the blue curves hugging the lower bounds.

abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have spurred significant interest in learning-augmented algorithms, particularly for online optimization. A growing body of work has studied online bidding in this framework, aiming to characterize the trade-off between robustness and consistency. While this trade-off is fully understood for deterministic algorithms, a gap between upper and lower bounds remains in the randomized setting. In this paper, we close this gap by presenting a Pareto-optimal randomized learning-augmented algorithm for this problem. Our approach introduces the notion of a bidding profile, a novel framework for representing the distribution over bids generated by an algorithm. We show that any bidding algorithm can be reduced, without loss of generality, to one driven by a bidding profile, and we characterize the optimal profile via a system of delayed differential equations. Finally, we demonstrate the broader applicability of our approach by extending it to the linear search problem, yielding a significant improvement over prior learning-augmented algorithms for linear search.
